texts./README.md: Kelpie A small command-line tool that backs up folders as snapshots. Each snapshot is a full picture of a folder, and only what changed since the last one is stored. kelpie init ~/backups/store kelpie snap ~/documents kelpie restore latest --to ~/restored Start here Install · Your first backup · Commands · Configuration Going further Stores: a local disk, SFTP or object storage. Recipes: a nightly backup with cron, a laptop to a NAS, moving a store. How Kelpie works: chunks, snapshots, retention, encryption and the store's format. When something goes wrong Troubleshooting · Questions people ask The current version is 0.9.2. What changed is in the changelog. Kelpie is written in Go and released under the MIT licence. To help, read Contributing.
texts./commands/prune.md: kelpie prune Removes the snapshots that no retention rule keeps, and then the chunks that no snapshot uses any more. Synopsis kelpie prune [--store PATH] [--keep-last N] [--keep-daily N] [--keep-weekly N] [--keep-monthly N] [--dry-run] What it does 1. Reads the list of snapshots in the store. 2. Applies the retention rules, from the flags or else from the config file, and marks every snapshot that no rule keeps. 3. Removes the marked snapshots, and then every chunk that no remaining snapshot refers to. Flags Flag Meaning Default --store PATH the store to prune the store named in the config file --keep-last N, --keep-daily N, --keep-weekly N, --keep-monthly N the retention rules, explained on the retention page the rules in the config file --dry-run prints what would be removed, and removes nothing off Exit codes 0 the store was pruned 1 an error, and nothing was removed Notes Prune needs the store's password, as every command that reads snapshots does. On a store over SFTP a prune takes longer than a snap, because the name of every chunk is listed first. See also kelpie verify, which checks that every chunk a snapshot needs is there.
texts./internals/retention.md: Retention: which snapshots are kept Every snap adds a snapshot. Retention is the set of rules that says which of them stay, and prune is the command that removes the rest. Why it matters A store only grows. In our own test store, one snapshot a night of a 40 GB home folder grew the store to 71 GB within a year. 58 GB of that was held only by snapshots older than three months. With the default rules the same store stays near 46 GB. If you have never run prune, you do not have a backup plan, you have a disk that is filling up. The rules A rule keeps snapshots. Nothing is removed because of a rule: what no rule keeps is removed. Rule Keeps Default keep-last N the newest N snapshots, whatever their age 3 keep-daily N the newest snapshot of each of the last N days that have one 7 keep-weekly N the newest snapshot of each of the last N weeks that have one 4 keep-monthly N the newest snapshot of each of the last N months that have one 6 A week ends on Sunday. Days, weeks and months are counted in the time zone of the machine that runs prune, not of the machine that took the snapshot. A worked example Take a store with one snapshot every night for 60 nights, and the rules keep-daily 7 and keep-weekly 4. After a prune, 11 snapshots are left: seven daily ones and four weekly ones. Run kelpie prune --dry-run to see the list before anything is removed. What prune never removes The newest snapshot of every folder stays, even when no rule keeps it. A folder you stopped backing up a year ago still has one snapshot. A snapshot with a tag stays until the tag is taken off. Tags are meant for the few snapshots you would be sorry to lose, such as the one from before a big migration. Some people tag every snapshot out of habit, which switches retention off without saying so. Retention decides what you can get back. Prune only carries the decision out. Three common setups Setup Rules Snapshots after a year A laptop keep-daily 7, keep-weekly 4 about 10 A home server keep-daily 14, keep-monthly 12 about 25 An archive keep-monthly 24, keep-last 1 12 Before you tighten the rules Tightening is the one change that cannot be taken back: a snapshot that prune removed is gone. Run the new rules with --dry-run first, and read the list. Loosening the rules is always safe. Next: Encryption

entries.text: I'm looking into what prune does while a snap is running.
I'm reading how prune and snap lock the store.

Prune cannot remove chunks of a snapshot that is still being written, as far as I can read the code. It works in three steps. First, prune asks for the store's exclusive lock, a file named locks/exclusive in the store. A snap holds a shared lock while it runs, so prune waits, for ten minutes at most, and then gives up with exit code 3. Second, once it has the lock, it marks the snapshots that no rule keeps and removes them. Third, it removes the chunks nothing uses, but never a chunk younger than 24 hours, so even the chunks of a snap that crashed before it wrote its snapshot stay for a day. So nothing an unfinished snapshot needs is removed: either prune waits for the snap, or the chunks are too young to go. There are two risks. A machine that dies while it holds a lock leaves the lock behind, and every prune after that gives up until somebody runs kelpie unlock by hand. And on a store over SFTP the lock is only a file that each side looks for, so two machines that start within the same second could both believe they hold it; I did not test that. What I would do: say on the prune page that exit code 3 means the store was busy; let a lock older than a day expire by itself; try two machines against one SFTP store to see whether that race is real; and bring the store format page up to date, which still describes a single lock.

The page's text:
<<<
Retention: which snapshots are kept Every snap adds a snapshot. Retention is the set of rules that says which of them stay, and prune is the command that removes the rest. Why it matters A store only grows. In our own test store, one snapshot a night of a 40 GB home folder grew the store to 71 GB within a year. 58 GB of that was held only by snapshots older than three months. With the default rules the same store stays near 46 GB. If you have never run prune, you do not have a backup plan, you have a disk that is filling up. The rules A rule keeps snapshots. Nothing is removed because of a rule: what no rule keeps is removed. Rule Keeps Default keep-last N the newest N snapshots, whatever their age 3 keep-daily N the newest snapshot of each of the last N days that have one 7 keep-weekly N the newest snapshot of each of the last N weeks that have one 4 keep-monthly N the newest snapshot of each of the last N months that have one 6 A week ends on Sunday. Days, weeks and months are counted in the time zone of the machine that runs prune, not of the machine that took the snapshot. A worked example Take a store with one snapshot every night for 60 nights, and the rules keep-daily 7 and keep-weekly 4. After a prune, 11 snapshots are left: seven daily ones and four weekly ones. Run kelpie prune --dry-run to see the list before anything is removed. What prune never removes The newest snapshot of every folder stays, even when no rule keeps it. A folder you stopped backing up a year ago still has one snapshot. A snapshot with a tag stays until the tag is taken off. Tags are meant for the few snapshots you would be sorry to lose, such as the one from before a big migration. Some people tag every snapshot out of habit, which switches retention off without saying so. Retention decides what you can get back. Prune only carries the decision out. Three common setups Setup Rules Snapshots after a year A laptop keep-daily 7, keep-weekly 4 about 10 A home server keep-daily 14, keep-monthly 12 about 25 An archive keep-monthly 24, keep-last 1 12 Before you tighten the rules Tightening is the one change that cannot be taken back: a snapshot that prune removed is gone. Run the new rules with --dry-run first, and read the list. Loosening the rules is always safe. Next: Encryption
